sec:categorical-action-notation:
Notation for the categorical action.

The following notation applies to the categorical action:

  • \mathrm{tr} \colon \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A) \to R is the categorical trace.
  • R_{\int} \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A) is the Frobenius--Ricci endomorphism: the curvature of the Frobenius form \int_A, defined by R_{\int} = (\mathrm{id}_A \otimes \int_A) \circ F_{\nabla_{\int}}, where \nabla_{\int}(a) = \int_A(a_{(1)}) \otimes a_{(2)} - a \otimes 1.
  • \mathrm{tr}_A \colon \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A \otimes \Omega^{\bullet}(A)) \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(\Omega^{\bullet}(A)) is the partial trace over the A factor.
  • \psi^* = \int_A \circ S(\psi) \colon A \to \mathbf{1} is the adjoint section.
  • D_\nabla = q^{-1}\nabla + (1 - q^{-1})\iota_\xi\nabla is the q-deformed covariant derivative.
ex:categorical-action-notation-su2:
Example Categorical-action notation for \mathrm{SU}(2). For A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) with Haar integral \int_A = \int_G, connection \nabla f = df + \mathcal{A} \cdot f, and state \psi \in A:

  1. Categorical trace: \mathrm{tr}(T) = \sum_m \langle j,m \mid T \mid j,m \rangle is the usual matrix trace.
  2. Frobenius--Ricci: R_{\int} measures curvature of the Haar integral itself. On \mathrm{SU}(2), R_{\int} = 0 in the classical limit q = 1.
  3. Adjoint section: For \psi \colon \mathbb{C} \to A, the adjoint is \psi^*(f) = \int_G \overline{\psi(g)}f(g)dg.
  4. q-deformed derivative: At q = 1, D_\nabla = \nabla. For q \neq 1, the Reeb component couples the connection to the contact geometry.
prop:qou-canonical-action:
Proposition Canonical action of a quantum observable universe. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe equipped with connection \nabla, aether parameter q, q-Hodge star \star_q, and state \psi \colon \mathbf{1} \to A. Then (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) determines a categorical action, unique up to a scalar \lambda \in R^{\times}:

  \mathfrak{S}_q = \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}_q),

where \mathcal{L}_q = \mathcal{L}_q(\nabla, \psi) is the categorical Lagrangian. The square of the Dirac operator decomposes as:

  \mathcal{D}_\nabla^{2} = q \cdot R_{\int} + \mathrm{tr}_A\!\bigl(F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla\bigr).

Applying the categorical trace term by term yields the gravity + gauge + matter decomposition:

  \mathfrak{S}_q = 
  \underbrace{\int_A \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl(q \cdot R_{\int}\bigr)}_{\text{gravity}} + 
  \underbrace{\int_A \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl(F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla\bigr)}_{\text{gauge}} + 
  \underbrace{\int_A\!\bigl(\psi^* \cdot \mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi\bigr)}_{\text{matter}}.

The categorical trace factors as \mathrm{tr} = \int_A \circ \mathrm{tr}_A, so all three summands share the same integration. The gauge term is the Yang--Mills curvature integral. The action \mathfrak{S}_q is the analogue of Hamilton's classical S = \int L\,\mathrm{d}t, with \int_A replacing integration over spacetime and \mathcal{L}_q replacing the Lagrangian density. The single scalar \lambda tracks the normalization of the Frobenius form \int_A, corresponding to the freedom in choosing physical units.
rem:canonical-action-obstruction: Remark Scalar-ambiguity obstruction of the canonical action. The observability axiom \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 ensures that the trace \mathrm{tr} \colon \mathrm{End}(A) \to R is faithful. No endomorphism is invisible to integration. Relaxing this condition allows hidden symmetries and introduces a nontrivial kernel in the trace. The obstruction to recovering a well-defined action is classified by the cohomology class \kappa \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B}) that obstructs lifting in the quantum-lifting sense.
def:categorical-hamiltonian:
Definition Categorical Hamiltonian and phase-space Legendre transform. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe over a commutative ring R with categorical Dirac operator \mathcal{D}_\nabla = q^{-1}\nabla + \hbar_q\,\iota_\xi\nabla (\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}, quantum Planck constant) and categorical Lagrangian \mathcal{L}_q(\nabla, \psi) = \mathcal{D}_\nabla^2 + \psi^* \otimes \mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A). Grouping terms by degree (2, 1, 0) in the Reeb contraction \iota_\xi\nabla decomposes \mathcal{L}_q = \mathcal{L}_2 + \mathcal{L}_1 + \mathcal{L}_0, where

\begin{aligned}
  \mathcal{L}_2 &= \hbar_q^2\,(\iota_\xi\nabla)^2, \\
  \mathcal{L}_1 &= q^{-1}\hbar_q\,\bigl(\nabla \circ \iota_\xi\nabla + \iota_\xi\nabla \circ \nabla\bigr) + \hbar_q\,\bigl(\psi^* \otimes (\iota_\xi\nabla)\psi\bigr), \\
  \mathcal{L}_0 &= q^{-2}\,\nabla^2 + q^{-1}\,\bigl(\psi^* \otimes \nabla\psi\bigr).
\end{aligned}

Energy in a quantum observable universe is defined as the Legendre transform of \mathcal{L}_q along the Reeb clock direction at two levels:

  1. Operator Reeb-velocity Legendre transform. Over any commutative ring R, the directional Euler Legendre transform D_v\mathcal{L}_q[v] - \mathcal{L}_q along v = \iota_\xi\nabla defines the velocity-form Hamiltonian endomorphism

      \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{vel}}(\mathcal{L}_q)
  = 2\,\mathcal{L}_2 + \mathcal{L}_1 - \mathcal{L}_q
  = \mathcal{L}_2 - \mathcal{L}_0 \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A),

    which cancels the degree-1 gyroscopic cross-term and Reeb-matter term without dividing by 2 or assuming that \nabla and \iota_\xi\nabla commute.

  2. Phase-space canonical Reeb-momentum Legendre transform. Scaling \iota_\xi\nabla \mapsto \omega\,\iota_\xi\nabla by a clock rate \omega and applying a linear categorical action trace \tau yields the clock polynomial L_{\mathrm{clock}}(\omega) = a_2\,\omega^2 + a_1\,\omega + a_0 with a_k = \tau(\mathcal{L}_k). Over a field K with 2 \neq 0 and a_2 \neq 0, the canonical Reeb momentum \Pi = 2\,a_2\,\omega + a_1 defines the categorical Hamiltonian

      H_{\mathrm{can}}(a_2, a_1, a_0; \Pi)
  = \Pi\,\omega - L_{\mathrm{clock}}(\omega)
  = \frac{(\Pi - a_1)^2}{4\,a_2} - a_0.

    Over an ordered field with a_2 > 0, H_{\mathrm{can}}(a_2, a_1, a_0; \Pi) = \sup_{\omega \in K}\bigl(\Pi\,\omega - L_{\mathrm{clock}}(\omega)\bigr), attained uniquely at \omega = (\Pi - a_1)/(2\,a_2). Evaluating at the unit canonical clock momentum \Pi = 2\,a_2 gives

      H_{\mathrm{can}}(a_2, a_1, a_0; 2\,a_2)
  = a_2 - a_1 + \frac{a_1^2}{4\,a_2} - a_0,

    retaining the first-order minimal Reeb coupling -a_1 and the second-order recoil correction a_1^2/(4\,a_2) inside the canonical shift \Pi - a_1.

Three unit charts of the primitive energy. With causal speed c_q = q^{-1}/\hbar_q = 1/(q - 1) and full-circuit Reeb tick t_P = \hbar_q^{-1} = q/(q - 1), every energy observable in this paper is a projection of H_{\mathrm{can}} in one of three unit charts connected by exact field identities:

Unit chart Clock / length normalisation Energy observable Exact conversion identity
Aether action / mass chart Full Reeb circuit \ell_P = \hbar_q\,t_P = 1 Static action \mathfrak{S}_q, holonomy mass \mathfrak{m} Base trace in K
Causal-cone / worldline chart Per-step cone speed c_q = 1/(q - 1) Rest energy \mathfrak{E} = \mathfrak{m}\,c_q^2 \mathfrak{E} = \mathfrak{m}/(q - 1)^2
Electronic / hadronic per-tick chart Planck circuit tick t_P = q/(q - 1) Hadronic scale \mathfrak{E}_0 \mathfrak{E}_0 = (\mathfrak{m}_e c_q^2)/t_P = \mathfrak{m}_e c_q^2 \hbar_q = \mathfrak{m}_e/\bigl(q(q - 1)\bigr)
sec:variational-equations-intro: The canonical action \mathfrak{S}_q depends on the Frobenius form \int_A, the connection \nabla, and the state \psi. Varying each yields one of the three classical field equations in categorical form: the categorical Einstein equation, the categorical Yang--Mills equation, and the categorical transport equation. The transport equation governs the spatial propagation of states, combining parallel transport and Reeb diffraction. Tracing this propagation through a double-slit geometry predicts a material-dependent torsion phase shift.
prop:variational-equations:
Proposition Variational equations of the categorical action. Let \mathfrak{S}_q be the categorical action. The three variational equations are:

  1. Gravity (vary \int_A): \delta\mathfrak{S}_q / \delta\!\int_A = 0 is postulated to yield the categorical Einstein equation (treated here as an independent hypothesis rather than derived by an explicit variation):

      R_{\int} - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int})\mathrm{id}_A =  T_q[\nabla, \psi],

    where T_q is the stress-energy endomorphism constructed from the gauge and matter terms.

  2. Gauge (vary \nabla): \delta\mathfrak{S}_q / \delta\nabla = 0 yields the categorical Yang--Mills equation:

      \nabla \star_q F_\nabla + q \cdot [F_\nabla, \star_q F_\nabla] =  J_\psi,

    where J_\psi = \psi^* \otimes D_\nabla\psi - D_\nabla\psi^* \otimes \psi is the matter current.

  3. Matter (vary \psi): \delta\mathfrak{S}_q / \delta\psi = 0 yields the categorical transport equation:

      D_\nabla\psi =  0.
prf:variational-equations:
Proof Proof of Variational equations of the categorical action. Each equation is obtained by computing \delta\mathfrak{S}_q = 0 with respect to the indicated variable, using the non-degeneracy of \int_A.

Item (1): Vary \int_A. The gravity term \mathrm{tr}(q \cdot R_{\int}) depends on \int_A through the Frobenius--Ricci endomorphism R_{\int}. Varying \int_A \mapsto \int_A + \delta\!\int_A and requiring \delta\mathfrak{S}_q = 0 for all \delta\!\int_A gives, by non-degeneracy of the categorical trace, R_{\int} - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int})\mathrm{id}_A = T_q[\nabla, \psi], where the stress-energy T_q collects the \int_A-dependence of the gauge and matter terms. The trace subtraction ensures \mathrm{tr}(T_q) = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int}) (the contracted Bianchi identity).

Item (2): Vary \nabla. The gauge term \int_A \circ \mathrm{tr}_A(F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla) depends on \nabla through F_\nabla = \nabla^2. A standard computation using \delta F_\nabla = \nabla(\delta\nabla) and integration by parts (via non-degeneracy of \int_A) yields \nabla \star_q F_\nabla + q \cdot [F_\nabla, \star_q F_\nabla] = J_\psi. The commutator term q \cdot [F_\nabla, \star_q F_\nabla] arises from the non-commutativity of the q-deformed wedge product; it vanishes when q = 1 (the abelian/classical limit).

Item (3): Vary \psi. The matter term \int_A(\psi^* \cdot D_\nabla\psi) is linear in \psi. Varying \psi \mapsto \psi + \delta\psi and using (\delta\psi)^* \cdot D_\nabla\psi = 0 for all \delta\psi gives D_\nabla\psi = 0 by non-degeneracy of \int_A and the dagger structure (positive definite dagger).
rem:wavefront-propagation:
Remark Wavefront propagation and the categorical Dirac equation. The categorical transport equation \mathcal{D}_ abla\psi = 0 governs the spatial propagation of a state \psi \colon \mathbf{1} o A through the quantum observable universe. It is the categorical analog of the classical wave equation.

The two terms of the categorical Dirac operator \mathcal{D}_ abla = q^{-1} abla + (1-q^{-1})\iota_\xi abla contribute distinct physical effects:

  1. Parallel transport (q^{-1} abla): The state \psi is covariantly transported along geodesics of the connection abla. At q = 1, this is the only term, and the wavefront propagates without transverse spreading.
  2. Reeb diffraction ((1-q^{-1})\iota_\xi abla): The Reeb contraction \iota_\xi couples \psi to the vertical contact direction, inducing wavefront spreading. The state acquires transverse amplitude proportional to the quantum Planck constant \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}.

The beam width emerges as a derived quantity, determined by the Green's function of \mathcal{D}_ abla on the instanton background. On a flat instanton (F_ abla = 0), the Gaussian beam waist w_0 is fixed by q and the source geometry. At a material boundary, F_ abla eq 0 and the wavefront diffracts around the edge. The on-shell condition \mathcal{D}_ abla\psi = 0 eliminates the matter term from the Lagrangian, leaving only the topological gauge sector.
sec:particles-intro: The transport equation \mathcal{D}_\nabla \psi = 0 selects on-shell solutions, but requires a formal definition of a particle. This section defines a particle as a q-harmonic form, read off the fermion--boson decomposition from the weight splitting, and treat observation as a structural operation acting on these solutions.
def:categorical-q-ext-deriv:
Definition Categorical q-deformed exterior derivative. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe. The q-deformed exterior derivative d_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A) is

  d_q =  q^{-1}d + (1 - q^{-1})\pi_V \circ d,

where d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A) is the differential of the non-commutative de Rham complex. The q-adjoint \delta_q \colon \Omega^{k+1}(A) \to \Omega^k(A) is the formal adjoint of d_q with respect to the dagger structure.
rem:categorical-q-ext-deriv-remark: Remark Action of d_q on horizontal and vertical forms. The operator d_q acts as q^{-1}d on horizontal forms and as d on vertical forms. The operators d_q and \delta_q exist and are unique.
prop:categorical-q-ext-deriv-exists:
Proposition Existence of the categorical q-exterior derivative. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with connection \nabla, aether parameter q, and weight decomposition (\pi_H, \pi_V). Then the q-deformed exterior derivative

  d_q \;=\; q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1})  \pi_V \circ d
  \;\colon\; \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)

exists as a morphism in \mathbf{C} for every k.

Uniqueness is established separately in the uniqueness of the categorical q-exterior derivative (next proposition).
prf:categorical-q-ext-deriv-exists: Proof Proof of existence of the categorical q-exterior derivative. Build d_q as a scalar-weighted linear combination of the categorical de Rham differential d and its vertical projection \pi_V \circ d. d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A) is the non-commutative de Rham differential, part of the categorical connection data. \pi_V is a morphism by the weight decomposition. The scalar q^{-1} and (1 - q^{-1}) act via the aether parameter, and scalar multiplication and addition of morphisms exist in any R-linear category. The composite d_q is therefore a morphism in \mathbf{C}.
prop:categorical-q-ext-deriv-unique:
Proposition Uniqueness of the categorical q-exterior derivative. Given fixed d, \pi_V, and q, the categorical q-exterior derivative

  d_q \;=\; q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1})  \pi_V \circ d

is the unique morphism satisfying:

  1. d_q = q^{-1} d on horizontal forms \pi_H(\Omega^k(A));
  2. d_q = d on vertical forms \pi_V(\Omega^k(A));
  3. d_q is R-linear in the components.

Archimedean specialisation. What follows sits on the archimedean side of the algebraic→archimedean wall: it invokes real- or complex-analytic constructs — real-valued physical observables, real-analytic bounds, transcendental constants, or numerical evaluation at the aether parameter q_0. Any generic categorical / q-deformation identities it draws on remain valid over an abstract coefficient ring; only their archimedean realisation is specialised here.
prf:categorical-q-ext-deriv-unique: Proof Proof of uniqueness of the categorical q-exterior derivative. Any morphism d' satisfying (1), (2), (3) must agree with d_q on horizontal forms (q^{-1} d by hypothesis) and on vertical forms (d by hypothesis). Since \pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id} (weight decomposition), every form decomposes uniquely as a sum of horizontal and vertical parts, and R-linearity extends d' to the whole space by the formula d' = q^{-1} d \circ \pi_H + d \circ \pi_V = d_q. Hence d' = d_q.
def:q-harmonic-form: Definition Particle (q-harmonic form). Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with q-deformed exterior derivative d_q. The q-Laplacian on \Omega^k(A) is \Delta_q = d_q\delta_q + \delta_qd_q. A particle is an element \alpha \in \Omega^k(A) that is q-harmonic: \Delta_q \alpha = 0.
def:fermion-boson-decomposition:
Definition Fermion--Boson decomposition. Let \mathcal{H}_q^k = \ker\Delta_q \subset \Omega^k(A) denote the space of particles. The weight decomposition restricts to a short exact sequence

  0 \to \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k \to \mathcal{H}_q^k \xrightarrow{\pi_V} \mathcal{H}_{q,V}^k \to 0,

where \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k = \mathcal{H}_q^k \cap \Omega^k_H(A) and \mathcal{H}_{q,V}^k = \pi_V(\mathcal{H}_q^k). A boson is a particle in the kernel \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k (purely horizontal: \alpha_V = 0). A fermion is a particle with \alpha_V \neq 0. The sequence splits via \pi_H, giving the fermion--boson decomposition \mathcal{H}_q^k \cong \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k \oplus \mathcal{H}_{q,V}^k.
def:categorical-point: Definition Categorical point. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum universe. A categorical point of A is a morphism p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A. The augmentation ideal at p is \mathfrak{m}_p = \ker(p^* \colon A \to \mathbf{1}), and the germ of A at p is the quotient A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2.
rem:categorical-point-remark: Remark Categorical points in the archimedean realisation. In the archimedean realisation A = C^\infty(M), a categorical point p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A corresponds to evaluation at a point p \in M.
sec:categorical-point-explication:
Points in the archimedean realisation.

In the archimedean realisation A = \mathcal{O}(G), a categorical point p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A is a character \mathrm{ev}_g \colon f \mapsto f(g) for some g \in G; equivalently, a point of the group G. For a manifold M with A = C^{\infty}(M), a point p corresponds to evaluation at p \in M:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:point-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  \{*\} \ar[r, "p"]
  & M
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em]
  \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "p"]
  & A
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

The augmentation ideal at p is \mathfrak{m}_p = \ker(p^* \colon A \to \mathbf{1}), where p^* = \int_A \circ \mu(p \otimes -). The germ of A at p is the quotient A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2, which captures the first-order behaviour of A near p.
def:observation:
Definition Observation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with state bundle \mathcal{S} \to M, and let p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A be a categorical point. Let R be a commutative ring containing \mathbb{Q}, let h = q - q^{-1}, and let H_n = H_n(R[[h]], q) be the Hecke algebra over the formal power series ring in h. Write

  W_1 = \mathrm{span}\{\sigma_0,\ \sigma_1,\ \sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1}\} \subset H_3

for the span of the three non-identity terms of the photon \gamma = 1 + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\,\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} (the photon is defined in the chapter on Bring's surface).

An observation at p (also called an intent at p) is a pair (w_p, \delta q_p) consisting of:

  1. A probe direction w_p \in h\,W_1[[h]]. It acts on a closed state \psi by conjugation, \psi \mapsto e^{w_p}\,\psi\,e^{-w_p}. The exponential converges in the h-adic topology because w_p is divisible by h. The first-order change is the commutator [w_p, \psi]. Conjugation preserves every trace, so the Frobenius form is preserved.
  2. An aether deformation \delta q_p \in R, which shifts the aether parameter q \mapsto q' = q + \delta q_p.

Two observations at the same point with directions w_1, w_2 fail to commute by

  e^{w_1} e^{w_2} e^{-w_1} e^{-w_2} = 1 + [w_1, w_2] + O(h^3),

and the first-order term [w_1, w_2] is the q-curvature of the two-observer parallelogram (see the remark that follows).

The direction w_p is a vector in a 3-dimensional space, not a choice between a forward crossing \sigma_i and a backward crossing \sigma_i^{-1}. The first-order data are taken in h\,W_1 rather than in the 1-jet space \mathfrak{m}_p/\mathfrak{m}_p^2 because that space is zero at any character of a semisimple Hecke fibre: (\sigma - q)^2 = -(q + q^{-1})(\sigma - q), so \sigma - q \in \mathfrak{m}_p^2 whenever q + q^{-1} is invertible.
rem:observation-physical-roles:
Remark Physical roles of the observation components. The two components of an observation correspond to its two physical roles:

  • Receiving: the J^1 (jet) component reads the field --- a local section of the state bundle \mathcal{S} --- and its first derivative: position and linear approximation. This is the inflow of information from the state bundle, through the affine chart (fibre functor atlas) centred on U.

  • Sending back: the \mathrm{Ad} (adjoint) component acts on the colour fibre by conjugation, rotating the gauge degrees of freedom. This is the backreaction: the observation perturbs q, which shifts the Reeb flow, which changes what the next observation reads.

The direction w_p \in h\,W_1[[h]] of an observation determines which combination of the crossings \sigma_0, \sigma_1 and the vertex \sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1} the probe injects at p. A forward crossing \sigma_i and a backward crossing \sigma_i^{-1} = \sigma_i - h differ by a multiple of the identity, so as probe directions they act identically by conjugation.
prop:observation-energy:
Proposition Observation increases quantum energy and deforms the action. Let \mathfrak{O} be an observation with positive aether perturbation \delta q > 0. The quantum Planck constant \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} satisfies

  \hbar_{q + \delta q} - \hbar_q =  \frac{\delta q}{q(q + \delta q)} >  0.

Every observation with positive aether perturbation strictly increases the quantum energy of the system.

The categorical action evaluated at the perturbed parameter q' = q + \delta q satisfies

  \mathfrak{S}_{q'} = \mathfrak{S}_q +  \delta q \cdot \frac{\partial \mathfrak{S}_q}{\partial q} + O((\delta q)^2).

The first-order shift is the observation cost. The classical energy can increase or decrease under observation; only the quantum energy monotonically increases.
prf:observation-energy:
Proof Proof of Observation increases quantum energy and deforms the action. (1) \hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} is strictly increasing in q for q > 0. Its derivative d\hbar_q/dq = q^{-2} > 0. Hence \delta q > 0 implies \delta\hbar_q > 0.

(2) Direct Taylor expansion of \mathfrak{S}_{q'} about q.

(3) The classical action \mathfrak{S}_1 = \lim_{q \to 1} \mathfrak{S}_q depends on \nabla, \lambda, \psi but not on q. An observation that changes \nabla or \psi while holding q fixed modifies the classical energy by the variational equations (Einstein, Yang--Mills, transport). The sign of this modification is unconstrained --- it depends on the observer's choice of how to act on the state bundle. The continuity requirement is the Frobenius compatibility axiom: the observation must preserve the trace. \square
rem:two-observer-parallelogram:
Remark Two-observer parallelogram. Let p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A be a categorical point. Consider two independent observations at p with probe directions w_1, w_2 \in h\,W_1[[h]] acting on a fermion \alpha. To first order their discrepancy is

  [w_1, w_2] \cdot (\alpha_V)_p.

This vanishes if and only if the two directions commute or the particle is a boson ((\alpha_V)_p = 0). The Hecke algebra is non-commutative, so [w_1, w_2] \neq 0 for generic directions, for example w_1 = h\sigma_0 and w_2 = h\sigma_1: independent observations of a fermion at the same point generically disagree.

At a point p, the commutator of two observations equals the q-curvature F_q of the q-connection evaluated on the loop spanned by the two observation directions: [w_1, w_2] = F_q. The observers agree if and only if the q-curvature vanishes. Swapping the observers negates the curvature.
prop:germ-commutator-q-curvature:
Proposition Germ-commutator of two observations equals the q-curvature on the loop. At a point p, let two independent observations (observation) have probe directions \delta q_1 := w_1 and \delta q_2 := w_2 in h\,W_1[[h]], viewed as increments in the non-commutative Hecke algebra H_n(R[[h]], q). Their commutator equals the q-curvature F_q of the q-connection (a q-flat connection, defined in the q-Geometric Langlands chapter) evaluated on the loop spanned by the two observation directions:

  [\delta q_1,\, \delta q_2] \;=\; F_q.

This is the formal core of the two-observer parallelogram (two-observer parallelogram): the local disagreement between two observers is the q-curvature on the infinitesimal loop they trace. Two structural consequences follow.

  1. Agreement \iff flatness. The observers agree ([\delta q_1, \delta q_2] = 0) iff the q-curvature vanishes, F_q = 0 — the boson / q-flat case. Generically the non-cocommutativity of the Hopf structure forces F_q \neq 0, so independent fermionic observations at the same point necessarily disagree.
  2. Antisymmetry. Swapping the two observers negates the curvature, F_q \mapsto -F_q: the curvature is a genuine 2-form on the loop.

The germ algebra's non-commutativity is exactly what makes the commutator, and hence F_q, non-trivial; over a commutative ring the parallelogram would close and F_q would vanish identically.

The identity [\delta q_1, \delta q_2] = F_q is unconditional (structural); the identification of F_q with the intrinsic q-curvature (q-1)\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}} of the q-flat connection is the narrative bridge. Together these promote the parallelogram's \delta q(p) to the curvature of the q-connection — the kinematic half of how the aether parameter q evolves locally at a point.
conj:q-harmonic-flow:
Conjecture The aether field q(p) evolves by the q-harmonic-map heat flow \partial_t q = -\Delta_q q. The aether parameter q(p) is conjectured to evolve by the q-harmonic-map heat flow:

  \partial_t\, q \;=\; -\,\Delta_q\, q,
  \qquad
  \Delta_q \;=\; q^{-2}\Delta \;+\; q^{-1}(1-q^{-1})\,\mathfrak{C}
            \;+\; (1-q^{-1})^2\,\Delta_\xi ,

where \Delta is the base Laplacian, \mathfrak{C} the first-order Casimir/drift term, and \Delta_\xi the Reeb-fibre Laplacian. Its stationary configurations \Delta_q q = 0 are the q-harmonic sections; the vacuum constant q \equiv q_0 is the trivial one. This PDE serves as an ansatz for the dynamical evolution of the aether parameter.
rem:observation-fermion-action:
Remark The observer acts directly on fermions via the colour fibre. The \mathrm{Ad} component of an observation acts directly on fermions via the eigenspace decomposition of the Hecke generator \sigma:

  V \otimes V = \underbrace{\mathrm{Sym}^2(V)}_{\text{bosonic, } q} \oplus \underbrace{\textstyle\bigwedge^2(V)}_{\text{fermionic, } {-q^{-1}}}

On bosons (\mathrm{Sym}^2), the observation preserves the eigenspace. The \mathrm{Ad} action commutes with the symmetric projection. The commutator of two observations vanishes on bosons. Bosons can be observed without interference.

On fermions (\bigwedge^2), the \mathrm{Ad} action conjugates the antisymmetric component by G, mixing the fermionic state with the bosonic eigenspace. The observation partially converts fermionic content to bosonic content, depositing q + q^{-1} per crossing in the colour fibre. Two observers acting on the same fermion interfere because their rotations in the colour fibre do not commute. The geometric non-commutativity of G = \mathrm{SU}_2(R) forces this uncertainty.
sec:geometric-interpretations-intro:
This section interprets the categorical operators d_q, \delta_q, \Delta_q, and the fermion--boson decomposition through the dictionary of classical vector calculus. The q-Laplacian \Delta_q \alpha = 0 identifies equilibrium between the spatial environment and internal quantum spin. The closed form \delta_q = q^{-1}\delta + (1-q^{-1}) \mathcal{L}_\xi^* \circ \iota_\xi enables a three-term expansion of \Delta_q into classical diffusion, Coriolis cross-coupling, and pure spin diffusion.

A particle is simultaneously q-closed and q-coclosed. Allowing q to acquire a phase destroys the positivity of the Haar functional and is excluded by the observability axiom, but the algebraic sector remains internally consistent.
rem:vector-calculus-bridge:
Remark Differential forms and the classical vector calculus operators. Recall the classical vector calculus operators as differential forms on a smooth Riemannian manifold (M, g).

A 0-form is a scalar field f \colon M \to \mathbb{R}. A 1-form \alpha assigns a number to each tangent vector. A 2-form \beta measures oriented flux through an infinitesimal parallelogram.

The exterior derivative d yields the gradient df on a 0-form and the curl d\alpha on a 1-form. The identity d^2 = 0 encodes \nabla \times (\nabla f) = 0 and \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) = 0.

The Hodge star \star maps k-forms to (n{-}k)-forms by complementing directions. The codifferential \delta = (-1)^{nk+n+1}\star d\star is the formal adjoint of d, acting as -\mathrm{div}(\alpha^{\sharp}) on 1-forms. The Hodge Laplacian is \Delta = d\delta + \delta d. A function f is harmonic (\Delta f = 0) when its value equals the average over any small sphere centered at the point.
rem:q-laplacian-interpretation:
Remark The q-Laplacian as quantum averaging. The q-Laplacian \Delta_q = d_q\delta_q + \delta_qd_q replaces the classical neighbourhood with a quantum-twisted neighbourhood that weights the horizontal (spatial) and vertical (Reeb/spin) directions differently.

Setting \Delta_q \alpha = 0 specifies that the field \alpha is in equilibrium between its spatial environment and its internal quantum spin. The geometric twist precisely counterbalances the spatial diffusion:

  • At q = 1: d_q = d, and \Delta_q reduces to the Hodge Laplacian \Delta. The quantum twist vanishes, and q-harmonic forms are ordinary harmonic forms.
  • At q \to \infty: d_q projects onto \pi_V \circ d. A q-harmonic form is averaged purely along the internal fibre.

A q-harmonic form (\Delta_q \alpha = 0) is a particle: a field configuration in perfect q-equilibrium with its twisted geometric environment. The aether parameter q tunes the relative weight of spatial diffusion versus internal spin.
prop:q-codifferential-formula:
Proposition Closed formula for the q-codifferential \delta_q. Let d_q = q^{-1}d + (1 - q^{-1})\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi be the q-exterior derivative. The formal adjoint of d_q with respect to the Tanaka–Webster inner product \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_\varTheta is

  \delta_q =  q^{-1}\delta +  (1 - q^{-1})\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \circ \iota_\xi.

This is uniquely characterised by the adjoint relation \langle d_q\alpha, \beta \rangle_\varTheta = \langle \alpha, \delta_q\beta \rangle_\varTheta for all compactly supported forms \alpha, \beta.
rem:q-codifferential-formula:
Remark Expanded formula for the q-codifferential \delta_q. In the archimedean realisation, the q-exterior derivative is d_q = q^{-1}d + (1 - q^{-1})\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi. To find the formal adjoint \delta_q, each operation in d_q is replaced by its geometric mirror:

  1. The derivative d becomes the codifferential \delta.
  2. Wedging with the contact form (\varTheta \wedge) becomes contraction with the Reeb vector field (\iota_\xi).
  3. The Lie derivative \mathcal{L}_\xi becomes its formal adjoint \mathcal{L}_\xi^*.

The closed formula is \delta_q = q^{-1}\delta + (1 - q^{-1})\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \circ \iota_\xi. While d_q uses the Reeb vector field to add a vertical spin twist, the codifferential \delta_q uses contraction with \xi to extract it.
rem:q-laplacian-expansion:
Remark Three-term expansion of the q-Laplacian. Expanding \Delta_q = d_q\delta_q + \delta_qd_q separates the q-Laplacian into three terms:

  1. Classical core (\propto q^{-2}): Proportional to q^{-2}\Delta, this is the standard spatial diffusion operator.
  2. Quantum spin core (\propto (1 - q^{-1})^2): Involving only Reeb operations (\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi and \mathcal{L}_\xi^* \circ \iota_\xi), these terms represent pure internal Reeb dynamics.
  3. Cross-coupling terms (\propto q^{-1}(1 - q^{-1})): Mixed terms combining spatial derivatives with Reeb operations measure the interference between macroscopic spatial motion and internal spin.

The expansion is:

  \Delta_q = q^{-2}\Delta +  q^{-1}(1 - q^{-1})\bigl[d(\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \iota_\xi) + (\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi)\delta + \delta(\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi) + (\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \iota_\xi)d\bigr] +  (1 - q^{-1})^2\Delta_{\xi},

where \Delta_\xi = (\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi) (\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \iota_\xi) + (\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \iota_\xi) (\varTheta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi) is the pure spin Laplacian.
prop:q-laplacian-spectral-tower:
Proposition The q-Laplacian spectral tower [k]_q^2 and its root-of-unity (Verlinde/ADE) truncation. The q-Laplacian \Delta_q has eigenvalues given by the q-integer tower

  [k]_q^2, \qquad [k]_q = \frac{q^k - q^{-k}}{q - q^{-1}} \quad (k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots).

At a primitive root of unity q = e^{i\pi/r}, the q-integer [r]_q vanishes, and the spectrum truncates to the finite set

  \{\,[1]_q^2, [2]_q^2, \ldots, [r-1]_q^2\,\},

yielding the Verlinde / ADE quantum-dimension data of the truncated representation category. The surviving quantum dimensions are exact algebraic numbers in the cyclotomic field \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_r). By Kazhdan–Lusztig [kazhdan-lusztig1993-tensor-i], the semisimplified truncated category is the modular tensor category of level-(r-2) \mathrm{SU}(2) Wess–Zumino–Witten representations. That equivalence concerns representation categories only; no conformal field theory is constructed here, and the real aether value q_0 is not a root of unity, so it lies outside this truncation.
rem:q-laplacian-consumers:
Remark Consumers of the q-Laplacian spectral tower; fibre vs observable level. The q-Laplacian spectral tower acts as the organizing data for multiple q-deformed structures. The q-heat equation \partial_t u = -\Delta_q u dictates that mode k decays as e^{-[k]_q^2 t}. The q-Navier–Stokes dissipation exhibits eigenvalues [k]_q^2 \sim q^{2k}. The Markov trace / Gram blocks encode block quantum dimensions [2j+1]_q, and the lifting obstruction tower caps at r-1.

The exact truncation at roots of unity guarantees that spectral computations form finite exact sums with no series-truncation error. The tower and its truncation form fibre-level statements; the observable component requires evaluating at the real archimedean aether value q_0.
rem:hodge-laplacian-relation:
Remark Self-adjointness of the q-Laplacian. The q-Hodge star \star_q rescales the inner product by the aether parameter q, and the q-codifferential \delta_q inherits this deformation. The q-Laplacian \Delta_q is formally self-adjoint with respect to the Tanaka–Webster inner product.

Self-adjointness guarantees real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenspaces. The space of particles, \ker \Delta_q, is a well-defined subspace with a canonical complement.
prop:categorical-lichnerowicz:
Proposition Categorical Lichnerowicz: \Delta_ abla^q = \mathfrak{D}_ abla^2 + frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{Sc}_q. Let abla be a categorical connection on an adjoint bundle over the contact affine chart with Reeb derivation \xi and q-Hodge star \star_q. Let \mathfrak{D}_ abla = q^{-1} abla + \hbar_q \, \iota_\xi abla be the categorical Dirac operator, and \Delta_ abla^q the categorical q-Laplacian. On the categorical-instanton saddle \star_q F_ abla = F_ abla:

  \Delta_
abla^q  =  \mathfrak{D}_
abla^2  +  	frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{Sc}_q,

where \mathrm{Sc}_q is the q-scalar curvature. On the Bring background, the Reeb generator \xi = e_3 is parallel, forcing \mathrm{Sc}_q = 0 and simplifying the identity to \Delta_ abla^q = \mathfrak{D}_ abla^2. The q-scalar curvature \mathrm{Sc}_q = R + O(\hbar_q) encodes both the classical scalar curvature and the q-anomaly contribution from d_q^2 eq 0.
prf:categorical-lichnerowicz:
Proof Proof of categorical lichnerowicz. The classical Lichnerowicz formula D^2 = \nabla^*\nabla + R/4 on a spin manifold goes through three ingredients: (i) Clifford-multiplication structure of the Dirac operator, (ii) Bianchi-identity manipulation of the cross-term, and (iii) self-adjointness pairing the rough Laplacian against \Delta = d\delta + \delta d. All three lift to the categorical q-deformed setting essentially verbatim, with the substitutions \nabla \mapsto q^{-1}\nabla, \iota_\xi \mapsto \hbar_q \iota_\xi, and \star \mapsto \star_q.

Step 1: Squaring the Dirac operator. With \mathfrak{D}_\nabla = q^{-1}\nabla + \hbar_q \iota_\xi \nabla,

\begin{aligned}
  \mathfrak{D}_\nabla^2
  &=  q^{-2}\, \nabla^2  +  q^{-1}\hbar_q (\nabla \circ \iota_\xi \nabla + \iota_\xi \nabla \circ \nabla)  +  \hbar_q^2 (\iota_\xi \nabla)^2 \\
  &=  q^{-2}\, \nabla^2  +  q^{-1}\hbar_q\,\bigl\{\nabla, \iota_\xi \nabla\bigr\}  +  \hbar_q^2 (\iota_\xi \nabla)^2,
\end{aligned}

where \{\cdot, \cdot\} denotes the symmetric anticommutator. The last term \hbar_q^2 (\iota_\xi \nabla)^2 involves the second contraction along the Reeb direction.

Step 2: Clifford-multiplication identity. The Reeb contraction \iota_\xi acts as Clifford multiplication by \xi in the spin bundle (this is the categorical content of the d_q^2 \neq 0 anomaly — see q-Laplacian expansion). The Clifford relation \{\iota_\xi, \iota_\eta\} = -2\, g_q(\xi, \eta)\,\mathrm{id} applied with \eta = \xi gives (\iota_\xi)^2 = -g_q(\xi, \xi)\,\mathrm{id}, which on a unit Reeb vector field (g_q(\xi, \xi) = 1) reduces to (\iota_\xi)^2 = -\mathrm{id}. Combined with \nabla_\xi \xi = 0 (parallelism of \xi on the Bring background):

  (\iota_\xi \nabla)^2  =  -\nabla_\xi \nabla_\xi  +  \tfrac{1}{2}\,F_\nabla(\xi, \xi)  =  -\nabla_\xi^2  +  0,

where the curvature term vanishes by antisymmetry of F_\nabla.

Step 3: Anticommutator decomposes into Laplacian + curvature. The cross-term \{\nabla, \iota_\xi \nabla\} decomposes as

  \{\nabla, \iota_\xi \nabla\}
  =  \iota_\xi \nabla^2  +  \nabla(\iota_\xi)\, \nabla
  =  \tfrac{1}{2}\,\iota_\xi F_\nabla  +  \mathcal{L}_\xi \nabla,

using \nabla^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}F_\nabla (curvature definition) and \mathcal{L}_\xi = \iota_\xi d + d \iota_\xi (Cartan formula). On the categorical-instanton self-dual background \star_q F_\nabla = F_\nabla, the Reeb contraction \iota_\xi F_\nabla is in the +1 eigenspace of \star_q, so it contributes only to the symmetric part of \nabla^*\nabla, not to the antisymmetric d_\nabla \delta_\nabla piece.

Step 4: Assembly. Substituting Steps 2–3 into Step 1 and collecting:

\begin{aligned}
  \mathfrak{D}_\nabla^2
  &=  q^{-2}\, \nabla^2  +  q^{-1}\hbar_q\, (\iota_\xi F_\nabla/2 + \mathcal{L}_\xi \nabla)  -  \hbar_q^2\, \nabla_\xi^2 \\
  &=  \nabla^*\nabla  +  q^{-1}\hbar_q\,(\iota_\xi F_\nabla)/2,
\end{aligned}

after using q^{-2} - \hbar_q^2 = q^{-2}(1 - (q-1)^2) = q^{-2}(2q - q^2) = (2 - q)/q = q^{-1}(2 - q) and recombining the Reeb-direction terms with \nabla^*\nabla = \sum_\mu \nabla_\mu^* \nabla_\mu (the rough Laplacian).

The cross-term q^{-1}\hbar_q (\iota_\xi F_\nabla)/2 is exactly the q-scalar curvature contribution \tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{Sc}_q in the deformed setting, where \mathrm{Sc}_q on the contact background is defined as the trace of the Reeb-direction part of the curvature:

  \mathrm{Sc}_q  :=  4 q^{-1} \hbar_q\, \mathrm{tr}\,(\iota_\xi F_\nabla)/2.

On the Bring background where \xi is parallel and the maximal-torus action is locally trivial, \iota_\xi F_\nabla = 0, so \mathrm{Sc}_q = 0 and:

  \mathfrak{D}_\nabla^2  =  \nabla^*\nabla.

Finally, the Weitzenböck identity for 1-forms gives \Delta_\nabla^q = \nabla^*\nabla + \mathrm{Ric}_\nabla^q. On the self-dual instanton background, \mathrm{Ric}_\nabla^q also reduces to the same scalar curvature term, so

  \Delta_\nabla^q  =  \nabla^*\nabla + \tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{Sc}_q
  =  \mathfrak{D}_\nabla^2 + \tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{Sc}_q. \quad\square
